Hampshire
HAMP-shur
n. (the southern county of Winchester and Southampton, whose bishop Stephen Gardiner was Mary's Lord Chancellor and the chief architect of the persecution)
From Southampton, Old English Hamtun, the home farm or settlement; the shire was Hamtunscir, now Hampshire.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Hampshire is the southern county holding the cathedral city of Winchester, ancient capital of Wessex and of England, and the port of Southampton. Its bishopric was the richest in the kingdom, and from 1531 it was held, with an interruption, by Stephen Gardiner. Gardiner was a lawyer and diplomat who had argued the king's divorce, accepted the royal supremacy and then defended the mass, transubstantiation and clerical celibacy against Cranmer in print; deprived and imprisoned under Edward, he was restored by Mary in 1553, made Lord Chancellor, and became the principal author of the policy that revived the heresy statutes and sent some three hundred people to the fire. He died in November 1555, five weeks after Ridley and Latimer burned. The county also holds Southampton, from which the Mayflower first put out in August 1620 before being driven back, and which later sent many emigrants. The dictionary names Gardiner as the clearest English case of the civil sword taken up for a doctrine, and holds the throne that frames mischief by a law to be the thing Scripture most sharply distinguishes from lawful magistracy.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a chancellor as a chief judicial officer; heresy as a fundamental error in religion; a statute as an act of the legislature; to recant as to retract; and boldness as courage.

expand to see more

CHANCELLOR, n. A judge; the president of a court of chancery; in England, the highest judicial officer of the crown.

HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.

STATUTE, n. An act of the legislature of a state, that extends its binding force to all the citizens.

RECANT, v.t. To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration; to revoke a declaration or proposition.

BOLDNESS, n. Courage; bravery; intrepidity; spirit; liberty or excessive freedom of speech.

Key Scripture

Psa 94:20 — "Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?"

Act 4:19 — "But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye."

Dan 3:18 — "But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up."

Pro 28:1 — "The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion."

Modern Corruption

Southern county of Winchester and Southampton, whose bishop Stephen Gardiner became Mary's Lord Chancellor in 1553 and was the principal author of the revived heresy statutes.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the legal persecution of conscience, and the dictionary names the mechanism rather than merely the cruelty. Gardiner did not act as a mob; he acted as Lord Chancellor, through parliament and the courts, reviving statutes and setting commissions to work, so that every burning had a warrant. The psalmist has a name for that exact arrangement and it is the sharpest thing in Scripture on the subject: “Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?” (Psa 94:20). A government that legislates an injustice has not made it just; it has added the abuse of law to the original wrong, and the dictionary insists on the point because the same machinery was later turned on dissenters by Protestants.

The second paragraph states the limit of obedience, which the Hampshire sufferers found and which Scripture fixes in advance. The apostles put the question back on the court that was forbidding them to preach: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19). The three in Babylon give the form of a refusal that is neither seditious nor negotiable, telling the king plainly “that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up” (Dan 3:18), and offering no resistance beyond the refusal itself. That is the pattern: no rising, no plot, no sword, and no compliance. What such men have, and what their judges generally lack, is stated by Solomon with some irony: “The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion” (Pro 28:1). Gardiner died with the fires still burning and the policy already failing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'aven (H205), iniquity; Greek akouo (G191), to hear or hearken; Hebrew batach-sense of confidence in Proverbs 28.

expand to see more

Hebrew kisse' (H3678) — a seat, a throne; “Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee”, Psalm 94:20.

Hebrew 'amal (H5999) — toil, trouble, mischief; “which frameth mischief by a law”, Psalm 94:20.

Greek dikaios (G1342) — right, just, righteous; “Whether it be right in the sight of God”, Acts 4:19.

Greek krino (G2919) — to judge, to decide; “to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye”, Acts 4:19.

Hebrew kephir (H3715) — a young lion; “but the righteous are bold as a lion”, Proverbs 28:1.

Usage

"“which frameth mischief by a law?” (Psa 94:20) — the heresy statutes revived in 1554."

"“that we will not serve thy gods” (Dan 3:18) — refusal without rebellion."

"“the righteous are bold as a lion” (Pro 28:1) — Gardiner dead in November 1555."
